Put the Phone Down: Why Drivers Should Not Use Cell Phones at the Wheel

Nearly everyone carries a phone now, and most of us reach for it dozens of times a day. That habit is exactly why the question of phones in cars matters. A car is a two-ton machine moving at speed, and the person controlling it needs to give it their full attention. My position is that drivers should not use cell phones in any capacity while operating a vehicle.

The strongest reason is how human attention works. People like to think they can multitask, but research on divided attention keeps showing otherwise. The brain switches between tasks instead of doing both at once, and each switch costs a moment of awareness. At highway speed, a driver who looks at a text for five seconds travels the length of a football field without watching the road. Nothing about that is safe, and no amount of experience makes a person immune to it.

Some people argue that hands-free calling is a fair compromise, since both hands stay on the wheel. The problem is that the danger is not only in the hands. A conversation occupies the mind. Studies of drivers on hands-free calls have found slower reactions to hazards and a tendency to miss things directly in front of them, a kind of tunnel vision. The driver may be looking at the road without really seeing it. A complete rule is also easier to understand and enforce than a partial one. If any use is banned, an officer or a passenger does not have to judge which kind of use counts as acceptable.

Others say phones are needed for navigation or emergencies. These are fair concerns, and they have simple answers. A route can be entered before the car starts, and a phone can be mounted and set to give spoken directions without being touched. If an emergency arises, the driver can pull over to a safe spot and make the call. Waiting a few minutes to stop costs very little compared with the cost of a crash.

Finally, driving is not a private act. A distracted driver endangers passengers, pedestrians, cyclists, and other drivers who never agreed to share that risk. Society already limits behavior that threatens others on the road, such as drunk driving and running red lights, and phone use belongs in the same category.

Changing a deeply ingrained habit is hard, but it is possible. Drivers can silence notifications, use a do-not-disturb mode, or place the phone out of reach. Every message can wait until the car is parked. A life is worth far more than a reply.
